entries.summary: E90 is the sedan body code for the 2005-2011 BMW 3 Series generation. The same platform also covers the E91 Touring (wagon), E92 (coupe), and E93 (convertible).
entries.body:
E90 is the sedan body code for the 2005-2011 BMW 3 Series generation. The same platform also covers the E91 Touring (wagon), E92 (coupe), and E93 (convertible).

Rear-wheel drive unless the car is badged xi, which means xDrive all-wheel drive. Front suspension is a double-pivot MacPherson strut design, rear is a multi-link axle.

The US-market 325i with the N52B25 engine was sold through roughly the 2006-2008 model years, before the LCI (facelift) update changed the front and rear lights, bumpers, and some interior trim.

Source: general public automotive reference knowledge. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, BMW made plenty of running changes within a single model year.

entries.summary: 2.5L naturally aspirated inline-6, one of the first BMW engines built with a magnesium/aluminum composite block instead of all-aluminum or iron. Uses dual VANOS (variable valve timing) and Valvetronic (variable valve lift, which lets the engine run without a traditional throttle plate for most operating conditions).
entries.body:
2.5L naturally aspirated inline-6, one of the first BMW engines built with a magnesium/aluminum composite block instead of all-aluminum or iron. Uses dual VANOS (variable valve timing) and Valvetronic (variable valve lift, which lets the engine run without a traditional throttle plate for most operating conditions).

Output is roughly 215-218 hp depending on market and model year.

Known wear points across the N52 family, not specific disasters, just things an owner this age should expect eventually:

- Electric water pump and plastic thermostat housing failures
- Plastic coolant pipes and expansion tank cracking with age and heat cycles
- VANOS solenoid issues causing rough idle or a check engine light
- Valve cover gasket seepage, usually shows up as a faint burning smell after the engine's been running a while

entries.summary: Replace the accessory serpentine belt that drives the alternator, water pump, power steering, and AC compressor.
entries.steps: 1. Note belt routing before removal (photo it) or check the routing diagram sticker under the hood. 2. Use a breaker bar or belt tensioner tool on the tensioner pulley bolt to release belt tension. 3. Slip belt off the pulleys, starting with the easiest to reach. 4. Inspect tensioner and idler pulleys for play or noise, replace if rough. 5. Route new belt per diagram, last pulley is usually the alternator or AC compressor. 6. Release tensioner slowly, confirm belt seats in all pulley grooves.
entries.torque_specs: Tensioner pulley mounting bolt: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact engine revision before using a memorized number
entries.part_numbers: Serpentine belt and tensioner/idler pulleys: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, revisions exist across production years
entries.tools_needed: Tensioner release tool or long breaker bar, flashlight
entries.notes_warnings: Double check routing before removing the old belt, a mis-routed belt can cause the AC compressor or alternator to spin backward. Replace tensioner and idler pulleys at the same time if they have any play, they're cheap compared to a belt failure on the road.

entries.summary: Replace a failed or failing alternator.
entries.steps: 1. Disconnect negative battery terminal first. 2. Remove serpentine belt (see serpentine belt procedure). 3. Disconnect electrical connector and B+ terminal nut from the alternator, note orientation. 4. Remove alternator mounting bolts. 5. Maneuver alternator out, it can be tight depending on what else is in the way on this engine bay. 6. Install new/rebuilt alternator in reverse order, torque mounting bolts and B+ terminal nut to spec. 7. Reinstall belt, reconnect battery, verify charging voltage with engine running.
entries.torque_specs: Alternator mounting bolts and B+ terminal nut: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec before using a memorized number
entries.part_numbers: Alternator: verify exact OEM part number against RealOEM.com using your VIN, and confirm whether yours has an integrated voltage regulator before ordering a replacement
entries.tools_needed: Socket set, possibly need to loosen other components for clearance depending on engine bay layout
entries.notes_warnings: Always disconnect the battery first, this is a live electrical component. Double check the B+ terminal nut is torqued properly, a loose one can arc and melt the connector. If charging voltage still looks wrong after replacement, check the battery and wiring before assuming the new alternator is also bad.

entries.summary: Drain and replace coolant, or replace the radiator if it's failed.
entries.steps: 1. Let engine cool completely before opening any part of the cooling system. 2. Remove engine undertray if present. 3. Open radiator drain petcock (or disconnect lower hose) into a drain pan, loosen expansion tank cap to help it drain. 4. If replacing the radiator, disconnect upper/lower hoses, electric fan connector, and remove radiator mounting. 5. Install new radiator if applicable, reconnect hoses and fan. 6. Refill with BMW-spec coolant mixed to the correct ratio, do not use a generic universal coolant. 7. Bleed the system per BMW's bleed procedure, this engine needs air purged properly or it will run hot. 8. Run engine to operating temperature with heater on full, check for leaks, top off after cooling.
entries.torque_specs: Radiator mounting and hose clamp fasteners: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec before using a memorized number
entries.part_numbers: Radiator, coolant (BMW-spec blue antifreeze, correct for this generation), thermostat and water pump if doing those at the same time since labor overlaps: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN
entries.tools_needed: Drain pan, BMW-spec coolant, possibly a cooling system bleed/fill tool for a cleaner bleed
entries.notes_warnings: This is the big one on N52-family engines: the electric water pump and plastic thermostat housing are known weak points, if you're already in here for a coolant change and either one is original, strongly consider replacing them proactively rather than coming back in a year. Never use non-BMW-spec coolant, the wrong chemistry attacks the plastic components in this cooling system.

entries.summary: Replace engine oil and oil filter as part of routine service.
entries.steps: 1. Warm up engine 5 min then shut off. 2. Remove engine undertray. 3. Remove drain plug, drain oil into pan. 4. Remove oil filter housing cap, replace filter element and both O-rings. 5. Reinstall drain plug and filter cap. 6. Refill with correct oil, check level.
entries.torque_specs: Oil drain plug: 25 Nm; Oil filter housing cap: 25 Nm
entries.part_numbers: Oil filter element: 11427566327; Drain plug washer: 07119963130; Engine oil: 5W-30 LL-01, 6.5 L with filter
entries.tools_needed: Oil filter housing wrench (36mm), drain pan, torque wrench
entries.notes_warnings: Don't overtighten the filter cap, it's plastic and cracks easily. Let oil drain fully, takes longer than people expect.
entries.source: my own experience doing this 10+ times

entries.summary: Replace front brake pads and inspect rotors.
entries.steps: 1. Loosen wheel bolts, jack up car, remove wheel. 2. Remove caliper guide bolts. 3. Lift caliper off, support with wire, don't let it hang on the brake line. 4. Remove old pads and anti-rattle clips. 5. Compress piston with tool. 6. Install new pads and clips. 7. Reinstall caliper, torque guide bolts. 8. Pump brake pedal before driving.
entries.torque_specs: Caliper guide bolts: 30 Nm; Wheel bolts: 120 Nm
entries.part_numbers: Front brake pads: 34116794914; Anti-rattle clip set: 34116765813
entries.tools_needed: Caliper piston tool, torque wrench, jack and stands
entries.notes_warnings: Reset the brake pad wear sensor if equipped, or the dash light stays on. Bed in new pads with a few gentle stops before hard braking.
